summary: OSPF Router LSAs always include advertised links in the default SPF computation, which is a problem for non-default computations such as Flexible Algorithms (RFC 9350). This Standards Track document uses the metric LSLinkInfinity to advertise links that the base SPF should not use. It updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379, and RFC 8770.

plainLanguage.summary: A map marks certain roads as "do not use for the normal route" yet still on the map for special trips.

questions: how to advertise unreachable links in ospf
subtitle: How OSPF can advertise a link that the normal route calculation must ignore, using the metric 0xffff.

tldr.problem: OSPF Router LSAs always include advertised links in the default SPF computation, so a link meant only for Traffic Engineering or a Flexible Algorithm still gets used for ordinary hop-by-hop routing.
tldr.mechanism: A link advertised with the metric LSLinkInfinity (0xffff) is treated as unreachable, but only once every router in the area has advertised a new Unreachable Link capability bit. Older uses of 0xffff move to a new value, MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe).
tldr.outcome: Operators can keep a link in the advertised topology while excluding it from the base SPF. The RFC updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379 and RFC 8770 so that their 'discourage use' metric becomes 0xfffe.

today: RFC 10041 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 5443, RFC 6987, RFC 8379 and RFC 8770.

sections.title: The Problem With Always-Reachable Links
sections.content:
OSPF Router Link State Advertisements (LSAs) use fixed-format encodings that always include advertised links in the default Shortest Path First (SPF) computation. A link may be needed for Traffic Engineering (TE) paths but not intended for hop-by-hop routing. Another example is a link used only by a Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350) and excluded from the default algorithm.

The fix is to advertise such a link with the metric LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), which marks it as unreachable. OSPF routers that support this document then leave it out of SPF calculations, subject to the backward-compatibility rules in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Some roads are built for special trucks only. The map needs a way to say 'regular cars, ignore this road' without erasing it.

sections.title: Use Cases: Traffic Engineering and Flex-Algorithm
sections.content:
In the first case, an OSPF link between Node A and Node E is only to be used for Traffic Engineering. Because the link is advertised by default, it is included in the base SPF calculation and may carry ordinary traffic in the default topology.

In the second case, the links between A and B and between C and D carry an Extended Administrative Group attribute with the color 'Red'. Flex-Algorithm 128 is enabled on nodes A, B, C and D with a rule that includes 'Red'. These links are reachable, so the default algorithm uses them as well. If their OSPF metrics are advertised as unreachable, they drop out of the base SPF topology and are used exclusively by Flex-Algorithm 128.
sections.plainLanguage: A school has a hallway for the band only. Everyone else is told the hallway is closed, but the band can still march through it.

sections.title: Treating 0xffff as Unreachable
sections.content:
If the OSPF metric of a link is advertised as LSLinkInfinity (0xffff), it MUST NOT be considered during the associated SPF computation. This applies to both the Flex-Algorithm SPF and the base SPF. The rule covers the Router-LSA and the Router-Link TLV of the OSPFv3 E-Router-LSA.

Before this document, OSPF treated a link with that metric as reachable. Supporting routers must therefore apply the new meaning consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest possible 'cost' number now means 'this road is closed to you', not 'this road is just very expensive'.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and the Capability Bit
sections.content:
Partial deployment can cause routing loops. In the RFC's example, link D-F carries 65535. Router B treats it as unreachable and routes to F via B, A, C, E, F. Router A does not understand the new meaning and sends traffic via A, B, D, F. A forwards to B, B sends it back to A, and the packets loop.

To prevent this, a router that supports the feature advertises a Router Functional Capability bit (bit 0, 'Unreachable Link') in an area-scoped Router Information LSA. Routers MUST NOT treat 0xffff links as unreachable unless every router with router-LSAs in the area has advertised the capability. When the count of non-supporting routers changes to 0 or from 0 to more than 0, all routers in the area MUST recalculate their routes.

While a new non-supporting router's Router Information LSA propagates, the routers can disagree about what 0xffff means. The RFC says this can cause transient routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody may treat a road as closed until every driver has said 'I understand the closed sign'. Otherwise some drivers would still use that road and others would not, and they would meet in the middle going in circles.

sections.title: The New MaxReachableLinkMetric
sections.content:
Several older specifications already used MaxLinkMetric (0xffff) to mean 'use this link only as a last resort'. That would now mean 'unreachable'. So MaxReachableLinkMetric (0xfffe) is defined. A router that supports the Unreachable Link capability MUST use 0xfffe instead in these cases:

  • Stub router links (RFC 6987 and RFC 8770): all non-stub links are advertised with cost 0xfffe.
  • LDP IGP Synchronization (RFC 5443): the link stays in the topology as a last resort for IP traffic while LDP is not fully operational.
  • OSPF Graceful Link Shutdown (RFC 8379): the link stays usable as a last resort before a planned shutdown.

If any router in the area lacks the capability, all routers treat 0xffff links as reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now a second sign: 'this road is open but only use it if you must'. It is a different sign from 'closed', so the old uses are not confused with the new one.

sections.title: Configuration and YANG Models
sections.content:
Support for the capability MUST be configurable, and by default the capability is not advertised. Some operators still want 0xffff links treated as reachable, for example when link cost is computed automatically from the inverse of bandwidth and a mix of slow and fast links yields the maximum metric. Implementations that support this document and auto-costing MUST therefore limit the computed cost to 0xfffe.

The RFC defines three YANG modules: iana-ospf-functional-cap-bits, ietf-ospf-functional-capability and ietf-ospf-unreachable-links. The last one adds an area-level enabled switch and a per-interface advertise-unreachable-link flag, both defaulting to false. The interface flag cannot be true unless the area switch is enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: The feature starts switched off. A grown-up has to turn it on, and an automatic cost calculator is told never to pick the 'closed' number by accident.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
A compromised OSPF router could flip its Unreachable Link capability rapidly, forcing repeated route recalculations. It is RECOMMENDED that routers supporting this document also support the SPF back-off delay algorithm of RFC 8405. The security considerations of RFC 2328, RFC 5340, RFC 6987 and RFC 7770 also apply.

For the YANG modules, writable nodes could be abused if unprotected: changes can stop 0xffff being read as unreachable or cause a link to be advertised as unreachable. Readable nodes may help mount Denial-of-Service attacks.

IANA registered bit 0, 'Unreachable Link', in a new 'OSPF Router Functional Capability Bits' registry, plus the XML namespaces and YANG module names for the three modules.
sections.plainLanguage: A troublemaker could keep flipping the 'closed' sign on and off so everyone keeps redrawing their route. Routers are told to wait a bit between redraws.

items.title: LSLinkInfinity 0xffff
items.text: Link is unreachable and is left out of SPF, once the whole area supports it.

items.title: MaxReachableLinkMetric 0xfffe
items.text: Link stays reachable but is a last resort; replaces 0xffff in stub router, LDP sync and graceful shutdown uses.
